summary: Exploratory study comparing four TDD interaction models on one toy Python task (a TextFormatter class that centres words in a line): solo human coding, human + GPT-3.5 Turbo collaboration, fully-automated GPT-3.5 Turbo TDD scripts, and the MetaGPT X agentic platform (GPT-5 or Claude Sonnet 4). Sixteen professionals (9 solo, 7 collaborative) took part in a static-group pre-experiment; the automated and agentic workflows were run repeatedly. Agentic output passed the most baseline tests and was fastest but was more complex with lower branch coverage; human-involved workflows produced better-organized tests.

claims.claim: Agentic workflow yields the most functionally correct production code
claims.evidence: Table 9: agentic > solo TPR U=106.5, p=7.81e-05 (significant after Holm-Bonferroni); mean TPR 94.58%. But agentic used GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4 while collaborative and fully-automated used GPT-3.5 Turbo (§4.2), so the model generation is confounded with the interaction model.

claims.claim: Agentic code introduces untested implementation decisions (higher complexity, lower branch coverage by baseline tests)
claims.evidence: §5.1.3 / §6: higher MCC and lower BCB; the 'untested decision points' interpretation is offered as 'one possible explanation', not verified by inspection of the branches.

claims.claim: Human-involved workflows produce better-organized test suites with higher coverage
claims.evidence: §5.2 / Table 16: solo-coding achieves higher statement and branch coverage than agentic; Kruskal-Wallis significant for SC and BC with medium effect (Table 8). n=9 and 7 humans on one task.
§5.3; MetaGPT X returned the solution in a single response because its SOPs do not support TDD-like iteration (§4.2.2), so it did not actually follow TDD and is not comparable on process.

patterns.note: Human-in-the-loop TDD gives better tests; the 'agentic' arm did not perform TDD at all (single response), so the study cannot speak to agentic TDD.
Human involvement improves test quality but costs time (assertion reformulation).
Notes agents add implementation decisions not required by the functional specification — a specification-completeness concern — but untested.

methodology.sample: 16 professionals (9 solo, 7 collaborative; 5 from a preliminary study plus 11 new); one two-subtask toy Python task; repeated autonomous runs (count per arm not clearly stated in extracted text)
methodology.baselines: Solo human TDD as control group; baseline test suite written by the authors
methodology.models: GPT-3.5 Turbo for collaborative and fully-automated; MetaGPT X Engineer mode with GPT-5 or Claude Sonnet 4 for agentic
methodology.variance: Means and SDs per arm (Table 16); Kruskal-Wallis and one-tailed Mann-Whitney U with Holm-Bonferroni; small-n acknowledged
methodology.ablations: Two prompt scenarios (minimal vs detailed) for agentic; merged after finding small differences
methodology.contamination_controls: None; trivial task likely well represented in training data

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint in Springer journal template (Received/Accepted placeholders); no venue stated
standards.artifacts: Prompts described in §4.3.1 and per-participant metrics in Appendix Table 16; no code repository link found

biases.detail: Single trivial TextFormatter task chosen to avoid complex APIs (§4.2).
9 vs 7 human participants in a static-group (non-randomized pre-test) design.
Agentic arm used GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4; collaborative and fully-automated arms used GPT-3.5 Turbo, so interaction-model effects are confounded with model capability.
The agentic platform produced a single response without TDD iterations yet is compared on TDD process efficiency.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: MetaGPT X, ChatGPT, Claude used as subjects; no ties
coi.funding: European Commission Next Generation EU, PRIN2022 2022TEPX4R (BeT) and Mission 4 Component 1
coi.detail: Academic authors with public funding; no vendor relationship found.

verdict_reason: One toy Python task, 16 participants, and a model-generation confound (GPT-3.5 vs GPT-5/Sonnet 4) between arms mean the comparison cannot isolate the interaction model; the 'agentic' arm did not perform TDD.
applicability: Little transfer to a Java multi-repo work team. The one usable hint — that autonomous agents add implementation decisions beyond the specification which the spec's tests then do not cover — argues for spec-driven development to pair every spec with acceptance tests and for a harness coverage check on agent-written branches, but this paper does not demonstrate it with credible evidence.
